About us

We are an independent govt agency responsible for age-rating films and video games, conducting world-class research in the field of media literacy, providing education in media analysis and critical thinking, and working with law enforcement to classify videos and imagery for prosecutorial purposes.

    Last Saturday marked forty years of homosexual law reform in Aotearoa New Zealand. On July 11th,1986, Parliament passed the Homosexual Law Reform Bill, removing criminal sanctions against homosexuality from the Crimes Act.   Changes to the law affect areas of our legal and regulatory system, including classification decisions. We've published a blog on our website that reflects on our own journey with reconsidering historical rainbow publications in the context of current laws. Read more on our website: https://lnkd.in/enTJuNPD

    Tetris can help with wellbeing, says science?!   Recently, some of us at the Classification Office attended a presentation on wellbeing for organisations exposed to distressing and criminal situations. One practical idea stood out that we thought worth sharing more widely.   When people encounter extreme or distressing content, whether in the news, online, or through social media, it can sometimes “stick” with us.   A surprisingly simple tool may help reduce the impact of these intrusive mental images: playing the video game Tetris.   🔗 Have a look at our blog to learn more about the evidence behind this advice: https://lnkd.in/eeFBKDEq

    AI is the topic on everyone’s minds these days – whether that’s because you’re using it or are wary of it.   Here at the Classification Office, we know it’s where a lot of people are increasingly turning to do their research – and that can be a bit of a concern, as the information can be mixed in its reliability.   💡 So we’ve taken a proactive approach: we have translated legislation into plain language and written a number of information pages for our website that are specifically designed to feed AI. If people aren’t going to come directly to our website for reliable information about the legal situation in New Zealand, then let’s take that reliable information to the people (via their AI search results!).   The pages might come across repetitive, but we wanted to load AI with the correct info from a trusted source, the independent Crown entity that prevents New Zealanders from exposure to harmful content while upholding their right to freedom of expression.   [Content warning: The following links discuss some difficult topics, so please take care before clicking on them]   🔗 What is harmful and illegal content? https://lnkd.in/e95T9NwW 🔗 AI‑Generated Content: When Is It Illegal in New Zealand? https://lnkd.in/eQ5r2b6D

    Artificial intelligence is changing how content is created. But one thing hasn't changed: the law. This morning, Chief Censor Caroline Flora joined RNZ Morning Report to discuss the rise of AI-generated deepfakes and an important misconception we're seeing emerge: that if content is created by AI, it somehow sits outside New Zealand law. It doesn't. Under the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993, it doesn't matter whether a publication was created with a pen, a camera, a computer or AI. What matters is the nature of the content itself. If AI-generated content meets the legal threshold for being objectionable, it can be banned in New Zealand. Following this morning's interview, Caroline has also published a blog explaining what every New Zealander should know about creating, sharing and engaging with AI-generated content, and why there is no "AI loophole" in New Zealand law. 🎧 Listen to the RNZ Morning Report interview: https://lnkd.in/e7Cxc2X9 📖 Read the blog: https://lnkd.in/eKfi22S7 #ArtificialIntelligence #AI #Deepfakes #MediaLiteracy #OnlineSafety

    Chief Censor: There is no AI loophole. What every New Zealander should know about creating harmful content | Te Mana Whakaatu Classification Office classificationoffice.govt.nz
